The problem

## Why does my tailbone hurt when I sit?

The coccyx, or tailbone, is the small bone at the very bottom of your spine. Every time you sit, and especially when you lean back, part of your weight rests on it. If it has been bruised, strained or pushed out of position by a fall, childbirth or long hours of sitting, that pressure turns into pain. Doctors call this **coccydynia**.

### Does this sound familiar?

- Pain right at the base of the spine

- Worse the longer you sit, or when you lean back

- A sharp jolt when you get up from a chair

- Pain during bowel movements or intercourse

It is very treatable, and most people never need surgery.

Why sitting hurts: leaning back loads the coccyx; leaning slightly forward moves your weight onto the sitting bones.

# Coccydynia (tailbone pain): symptoms, causes and self-check

Understanding coccydynia

## A small bone that can take over your whole day.

The coccyx is the last few small vertebrae at the base of your spine. It carries part of your weight every time you sit and anchors several muscles, tendons and ligaments of the pelvic floor. When it's injured, inflamed or out of position, the pain is called **coccydynia**.

It often follows a fall onto the backside, childbirth, long hours on hard seats, or repetitive strain like cycling or rowing. Sometimes there's no clear cause. Either way, it is treatable, and it rarely needs surgery.

🛝 Falls & direct trauma
🤰 Pregnancy & childbirth
💺 Prolonged sitting
🚴 Repetitive strain
⚖️ Sudden weight change
❔ No obvious cause

### Quick symptom check

Tick everything that sounds familiar. This is not a diagnosis, just a guide to whether a specialist consult makes sense.

Pain right at the bottom of the spine
It hurts more the longer I sit
Sharp pain when standing up from a chair
Leaning forward or to one side when sitting helps
Pain during bowel movements
Pain during intercourse or periods
Lying on my back is uncomfortable
I had a fall, injury or childbirth before it started

Select the symptoms that apply to you.

[Talk to a specialist](https://tailbone.netlify.app/book)

Medical facts

## What doctors know about tailbone pain

A plain-language summary based on leading medical references. It is general information and not a substitute for an examination.

### How common is it?

Tailbone pain is common. Women are affected around five times as often as men, partly because of pregnancy, childbirth and the shape of the pelvis. It is unusual in children.

### Usual causes

- A fall onto the backside, or another injury

- Pregnancy and childbirth

- Long hours sitting, especially on hard seats or while driving

- Repetitive strain, such as cycling or rowing

- Being well above or below a healthy weight; very flexible or very stiff joints

- Sometimes no clear cause is found

### Typical symptoms

- Aching or sharp pain at the very base of the spine

- Worse when sitting, leaning back, or getting up from a chair

- Pain with bowel movements or during intercourse

- Poor sleep and low mood when it lasts

### How it is diagnosed

Through your history and a careful examination of the coccyx and surrounding muscles. Before any hands-on treatment of a displaced coccyx, a dynamic X-ray (taken sitting and standing) shows which way it has shifted. MRI is used when needed to look for inflammation or other causes.

### Treatment options

- **Self-care:** a coccyx cushion, good posture with lower-back support, heat or ice, avoiding long sitting, softer stools

- **Hands-on therapy:** physiotherapy, pelvic-floor work and manipulation of the coccyx and its muscles

- **Injections:** local anaesthetic with steroid, when other measures don't help

- **Surgery** (removing part or all of the coccyx) is rare and kept for cases where everything else has failed

### Outlook

Most people improve within weeks with the right care. Pain that lasts more than a few weeks, or keeps coming back, deserves a specialist assessment rather than "just living with it".

### Dr Rajveer's five rules while your tailbone hurts

- **Sit on a firm cut-out cushion** Thick at the back, thin at the front, with a gap for the tailbone. A soft pillow doesn't help.

- **Get up and walk often** Every 30 minutes at work. Movement takes the pressure off the coccyx.

- **Stop cycling and bike riding** A narrow saddle puts your weight right under the tailbone.

- **No Kegels or squeezing exercises** Not until the direction of the shift is known: they can pull an inward-shifted coccyx further in.

- **No external "bone setting"** Pressing from outside can push a displaced coccyx deeper. The direction is checked first.

[Why the direction of the shift decides the treatment →](https://tailbone.netlify.app/blog/tailbone-subluxation-inward-or-outward.html)

### The research in numbers

Figures from published studies. The articles below explain each one, with full references.
Question What studies found Source

Women vs men About 5 women for every man Lirette 2014; Garg and Ahuja 2021
Started with an injury or fall 50–65% of patients Garg and Ahuja 2021
Sitting and standing X-rays Found a likely cause in 69% of 208 patients Maigne 2000
With ankylosing spondylitis 38% had tailbone pain, about 3 times the rate with ordinary back pain Deniz 2014
Women with pelvic pain Half also had coccydynia; 78% of them had a tight coccygeus muscle Neville 2022
Better without surgery About 9 in 10 Lirette 2014; Garg and Ahuja 2021

### ⚠️ See a doctor promptly if tailbone pain comes with:

- Fever or feeling unwell

- Numbness, tingling or weakness in the legs or around the buttocks

- New problems controlling your bladder or bowels

- A lump, swelling or wound near the tailbone

- Unexplained weight loss, or a history of cancer

- Severe pain after a major accident

For sudden numbness around the buttocks or loss of bladder or bowel control, go to an emergency department straight away.

While you wait for your visit

## Five small changes that ease tailbone pain.

1
### Lean slightly forward

Shifting your weight onto your thighs takes load off the coccyx.

2
### Use a cut-out cushion

A wedge or U-shaped cushion leaves the tailbone hanging free.

3
### Stand up every 30 min

Short breaks stop pressure and stiffness from building up.

4
### Avoid very soft sofas

Sinking in rolls you back onto the coccyx. Firm, supportive seats are better.

5
### Keep things moving

Fibre and water help prevent straining, which often aggravates the pain.

# Tailbone pain: frequently asked questions

FAQ

## Questions patients often ask.

### What is coccydynia?

It's the medical name for pain in and around the coccyx (tailbone). It usually gets worse when sitting, especially when leaning back, and when standing up after sitting.

### What is Internal Manipulation, and does it hurt?

It's a hands-on, non-surgical technique that frees up the tight ligaments and muscles attached to the coccyx and restores its alignment and movement. It is quick and done with full consent and privacy. Patients commonly report it's far less uncomfortable than they expected.

### How many sessions will I need?

It depends on your diagnosis, how long you've had the pain and your general health. Some people need very few visits, and others need a short course. We reassess your progress at every visit.

### What are the fees?

A consultation costs ₹800, at the clinic or online by video. A follow-up within 7 days costs ₹500. You pay at the clinic by cash, UPI or card. For an online consultation we tell you how to pay by UPI when we confirm the time. The cancellation and refund rules are on the [terms, fees and refunds](https://tailbone.netlify.app/policies.html) page.

### What should I bring to my appointment?

A short note of how and when the pain started, any past injuries or operations, and a list of the medicines you take. Wear comfortable clothing.

### Do I need a referral from a doctor?

No. You can book directly with us on the [contact page](https://tailbone.netlify.app/book), by phone or on WhatsApp.

### Is a female doctor available?

Yes. A female doctor, trained by Dr Rajveer Singh, sees patients at the New Delhi clinic. Just tell us when you call or message to book.

### I live outside India. Can you help?

Yes. Many of our patients travel from abroad, including from the Middle East. Start with an online consultation and we'll help you plan the visit.

### Can the doctor come to us?

Yes. On request, the specialist can travel to your city or country and treat you there, for one patient or a group. Travel, accommodation and food are covered by you, along with the treatment fee. Please ask at least 7 days ahead by phone or WhatsApp so we can plan the visit.

### How do I cancel or reschedule?

Call or WhatsApp us on [+91 98866 88323](tel:+919886688323) and we'll move or cancel it for you. The refund rules are on the [terms, fees and refunds](https://tailbone.netlify.app/policies.html) page.

# Tailbone pain, explained in pictures

A visual guide to coccydynia. Why sitting loads the tailbone, how it gets injured, how to tell it from other pain, what sitting and standing X-rays show, and how treatment is stepped up.

Tailbone pain (coccydynia) makes much more sense once you can see what is happening. This guide walks through it in pictures, one step at a time (moving diagrams and slides), with links to the full articles if you want to go deeper.

## Key points

- When you sit, your weight rests on **two sitting bones**. Leaning back or slouching adds the **coccyx as a third point**, and that is when it hurts.
- The coccyx is a small anchor for the **pelvic floor muscles, the buttock muscle and several ligaments**, so it is never just "a leftover bone".
- Pain usually comes from a **fall, childbirth or repeated strain** such as long sitting or riding over bumps.
- True coccydynia is pain you can **point to with one finger**, worst when sitting and when **getting up**.
- Sitting and standing X-rays compared side by side can show a coccyx that bends too far or slips. In one large study they found a likely cause in about **7 in 10** people.
- About **9 in 10** people get better without surgery.

## 1. A small bone with a big job

The coccyx is made of three to five small segments at the very bottom of the spine, joined to the sacrum above it. It is small, but it is an anchor point. The pelvic floor muscles that support the bladder and bowel attach to it, as do fibres of the large buttock muscle (gluteus maximus) and strong ligaments that tie it to the pelvis.

![Slide: the coccyx was once called a leftover organ, but it anchors the gluteus maximus, pelvic floor muscles, levator ani, sacrotuberous ligament and anococcygeal raphe, and helps carry weight when sitting.](/assets/img/blog/slides/slide-coccyx-anchor.webp "1280x714" "The coccyx is not a useless leftover: muscles and ligaments of the pelvic floor and buttock attach to it.")

That is why tailbone pain is often more than a bone problem. Tight or overworked pelvic floor muscles can pull on the coccyx, and a painful coccyx can make those muscles tense up in turn.

## 2. Why sitting hurts: the tripod

Sit up straight and your weight rests on the two sitting bones (the ischial tuberosities), with the coccyx held clear of the seat. Lean back, slouch or sink into a soft sofa, and the pelvis rolls backwards. Now the coccyx becomes the third leg of a tripod, and it is not built to carry that load.

This is why the simplest advice works so often: sit tall or lean slightly forward, and use a cushion with a gap at the back.

![Slide: when we sit, weight is spread across three points, the two sitting bones and the coccyx, forming a tripod.](/assets/img/blog/slides/slide-seated-tripod.webp "1280x714" "The pelvic tripod: two sitting bones and the coccyx.")

![Slide: upright posture sends weight through the sitting bones; slouched posture shifts the load onto the coccyx, causing repeated micro-trauma.](/assets/img/blog/slides/slide-slouch-effect.webp "1280x714" "Slouching moves the load off the sitting bones and onto the coccyx.")

Read more: [8 ways to sit more comfortably with tailbone pain](/blog/sitting-with-tailbone-pain.html)

## 3. Not every coccyx is the same shape

Some coccyges curve gently, others hook sharply forward, and in some the joint is already slightly out of line. Shape alone doesn't cause pain, but it changes how pressure is spread when you sit, so some people are more likely to develop problems.

![Slide: the coccyx is made of 3 to 5 small bones; its length, angle and curve vary greatly between people, which changes how pressure is absorbed.](/assets/img/blog/slides/slide-coccyx-variable.webp "1280x714" "Every coccyx is different in length, angle and curve.")

Read more: [Why some tailbones hurt and others don't](/blog/coccyx-shapes-and-movement.html)

## 4. How the coccyx gets hurt

| Route | Examples | What tends to happen |
|---|---|---|
| A sudden blow from outside | A fall onto the bottom on stairs, a wet floor or ice; a hard landing on a ride or water slide | Bruising, a sprain of the joint, a fracture or a joint that slips out of line |
| Pressure from inside | Childbirth, especially a difficult or assisted delivery | The coccyx is pushed backwards and the joint and ligaments are strained |
| Repeated strain | Long hours sitting, especially slouched; two-wheeler riding over bumps; cycling or rowing | Small, repeated overload that builds up without a single injury |
| Body weight at either end | Higher weight changes how the pelvis tilts when sitting; very low weight leaves little padding | Either can increase the load on the coccyx |
Table: Common ways the coccyx is injured. Sometimes no single cause can be found.

![Slide: acute trauma (falls, childbirth) causes fractures, sprains or dislocation; repetitive strain (long sitting on hard surfaces, cycling, rowing, long drives) causes slowly building inflammation.](/assets/img/blog/slides/slide-injury-mechanisms.webp "1280x714" "Two routes to injury: a sudden blow, or repeated strain.")

Read more: [Tailbone pain after having a baby](/blog/tailbone-pain-after-pregnancy.html) · [Two-wheelers, potholes and tailbone pain](/blog/two-wheeler-riding-and-tailbone-pain.html) · [Does body weight affect tailbone pain?](/blog/body-weight-and-tailbone-pain.html)

## 5. Recognising it

True coccydynia has a clear pattern:

- Pain right at the base of the spine, in the midline, that you can point to with one finger.
- Worse when sitting, especially leaning back, and often a sharp jab when **getting up** from a chair.
- Sometimes worse when opening the bowels or during intercourse, because the coccyx sits close to the back passage.

Pain mainly in one buttock, pain shooting down the leg, or numbness and tingling usually point somewhere else.

## 6. Is it really the coccyx?

| | Coccydynia | Pelvic floor muscle pain | Pain from the lower back |
|---|---|---|---|
| Where | The tip of the tailbone, in the midline | Deeper and more spread out; pressure in the back passage or vagina | Lower back, often spreading into the buttock or down the leg |
| Set off by | Sitting, leaning back, getting up | Stress, bladder or bowel problems, long sitting | Bending, lifting, long standing or sitting |
| Nerve signs | None | None | Sometimes tingling, numbness or weakness in the leg |
| What helps | Taking pressure off the coccyx; hands-on treatment of the joint | Relaxing and releasing the pelvic floor muscles | Treatment directed at the spine |
Table: Three common sources of pain low in the back, and how they usually differ. A careful examination tells them apart; they can also occur together.

A few less common conditions can feel similar, and some need other treatment. If you have fever, bleeding from the back passage, pain that is constant even at rest or at night, or unexplained weight loss, see a doctor promptly.

Read more: [Pain near the tailbone that isn't coming from the coccyx](/blog/tailbone-pain-mimics.html) · [When tailbone pain needs urgent attention](/blog/tailbone-pain-red-flags.html)

## 7. Seeing the problem: sitting and standing X-rays

An ordinary X-ray is taken lying down or standing, when no weight is on the coccyx, so it often looks normal. The French physician Jean-Yves Maigne developed a simple comparison: one side-on X-ray standing and one sitting. Comparing the two shows how the coccyx behaves under your weight.

In Maigne's study of 208 people with coccydynia, the two pictures showed a likely cause in about 7 in 10. A coccyx that bent too far (hypermobile) and a joint that slipped backwards were the most common findings. Backward slips were more common in people with a higher body weight, and small bony spurs at the tip in slimmer people.

Imaging is not needed for everyone. Most of the information comes from your history and a careful examination, and an X-ray is added when it will change the treatment.

Read more: [What happens at a coccydynia consultation](/blog/what-happens-at-your-consultation.html)

## 8. Which way has it moved?

When the coccyx is out of line, the direction matters. A coccyx pushed inwards and one pushed outwards need different hands-on treatment, which is why it is checked before anything is done.

Read more: [A displaced tailbone: why the direction of the shift matters](/blog/tailbone-subluxation-inward-or-outward.html)

## 9. Treatment, step by step

Treatment starts with the simplest, safest steps and moves up only if needed:

1. **Take the pressure off.** Sit tall or lean slightly forward, take breaks, and use a wedge or U-shaped cushion with the gap at the back.
2. **Hands-on treatment.** Treatment of the coccyx joint and release of the tight muscles around it, by a clinician trained in coccyx problems, with exercises to keep it moving well.
3. **Medicines** for short-term relief, when your doctor advises them.
4. **Injections or nerve blocks**, such as a ganglion impar block, for pain that persists despite the earlier steps.
5. **Surgery** to remove the coccyx, kept for a small number of carefully selected people because of its real risk of wound problems.

About 9 in 10 people improve with the first, non-surgical steps.

![Slide: mechanical pressure is eased by posture and cushions; muscle tension by physiotherapy; an irritated ganglion impar nerve centre by targeted nerve blocks.](/assets/img/blog/slides/slide-cause-and-solution.webp "1280x714" "Matching the treatment to the source of the pain.")

![Slide: everyday changes: manage constipation, pause cycling and rowing, avoid bumpy rides, and manage body weight.](/assets/img/blog/slides/slide-everyday-changes.webp "1280x714" "Everyday changes that take load off the coccyx.")

Read more: [How coccydynia is treated](/blog/coccydynia-treatment-ladder.html) · [Why "bone setting" can be dangerous](/blog/tailbone-bone-setting-risks.html)

## Summary

Tailbone pain is a mechanical problem with a clear pattern, and it can be worked out. Find out exactly where the pain comes from, take the load off the coccyx, treat the joint and the muscles around it, and step up only if needed. Most people get back to sitting comfortably without surgery.

## Sources

- [Maigne JY et al. Causes and mechanisms of common coccydynia: role of body mass index and coccygeal trauma. Spine. 2000;25(23):3072–3079](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11145819/)
- [Garg B, Ahuja K. Coccydynia: a comprehensive review on etiology, radiological features and management options. J Clin Orthop Trauma. 2021;12(1):123–129](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7920198/)
- [Lirette LS et al. Coccydynia: an overview of the anatomy, etiology, and treatment of coccyx pain. Ochsner J. 2014;14(1):84–87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3963058/)

# Why "bone setting" for tailbone pain can be dangerous

Pressing or massaging the tailbone from outside, without knowing which way it has shifted, can push an inward-displaced coccyx deeper into the pelvis. Dr Rajveer Singh explains the risk.

Many people with tailbone pain are taken to a local "bone setter" for an external massage or a quick push to put it back. Dr Rajveer Singh sees patients every month whose pain became worse afterwards. Here is why.

## Key points

- A displaced coccyx can shift **inward** into the pelvis or **outward**. From the outside, you can't tell which.
- If it has shifted inward, pressing on it from outside pushes it **deeper into the pelvis**: a small displacement becomes a bigger injury.
- Treating a displaced coccyx without first checking the direction on a **dynamic X-ray** is unsafe, and in Dr Rajveer's view unethical.
- A specialist realigns the coccyx with **internal manipulation**, aimed in the right direction.

## How a quick push can go wrong

The coccyx sits at the very bottom of the spine, partly hidden inside the pelvis. When it has been pushed inward (an anterior subluxation), the part you can feel from outside is already further in than it should be. Pressing on it from behind adds to the same force that displaced it. The muscles around it go into spasm, and sitting becomes even more painful.

| Before any treatment | What it shows |
|---|---|
| A careful history | How it started: a fall, childbirth, long sitting, a sudden jolt |
| An examination | Where it hurts, how the coccyx and the pelvic floor muscles respond |
| A dynamic X-ray (sitting and standing) | Which way the coccyx has moved, and how much it moves when you sit |
Table: What a specialist checks before treating a displaced coccyx.

## What safe treatment looks like

Once the direction is known, the coccyx is realigned by internal manipulation, gently and from the right side, in a short series of sessions. Exercises chosen for your type of shift then help keep it in place. See [tailbone subluxation: why the direction decides the treatment](/blog/tailbone-subluxation-inward-or-outward.html).

## If you've already had bone setting

Don't worry, and don't repeat it. If the pain is the same or worse, book an assessment. Many patients still recover well once the direction of the shift is known and treated properly.

## Sources

- [Dr Rajveer Singh's videos on tailbone pain (YouTube)](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCcLNy_lJceu4Ci8LaVW4GEw)
- [Garg B, Ahuja K. Coccydynia: a comprehensive review on etiology, radiological features and management options. J Clin Orthop Trauma. 2021;12(1):123–129](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7920198/)

# Kegel exercises can make tailbone pain worse

Kegels and "butt-squeezing" are often suggested for pelvic pain. Dr Rajveer Singh explains why they can pull an inward-shifted or fractured coccyx further out of place, and what to do instead.

Kegel exercises are good for many people, especially after childbirth. But if your tailbone has been pushed **inward**, or it is fractured, squeezing exercises can do harm. Dr Rajveer Singh asks his patients to stop them until the direction of the problem is known.

## Key points

- The pelvic floor muscles are attached to the coccyx.
- If the coccyx has shifted **inward** (an anterior subluxation) or is fractured, contracting these muscles pulls it further inside.
- So Kegels and "butt-squeezing" exercises should **not** be done until a specialist has checked which way the coccyx has moved.
- The right exercises depend on the direction of the shift, and are taught after the coccyx has been realigned.

## Why squeezing can make it worse

Several of the pelvic floor muscles, including the coccygeus and parts of the levator ani, attach to the coccyx. When they contract, they pull on it. With a normally placed coccyx that's fine. But if it has already been pushed into the pelvis, each squeeze tugs it further the wrong way. The displacement increases, the pain lasts longer, and treatment becomes harder.

| Exercise | Coccyx in normal position | Coccyx shifted inward or fractured |
|---|---|---|
| Kegel / squeezing exercises | Usually fine | Avoid: they pull the coccyx further in |
| What helps | Exercises a physiotherapist teaches you | Diagnosis first, internal manipulation, then direction-specific exercises |
Table: Squeezing exercises and the coccyx, as Dr Rajveer Singh advises.

## What to do instead

1. **Stop squeezing exercises** if you have tailbone pain and haven't been examined yet.
2. **Take the pressure off** with a cut-out cushion and regular breaks from sitting (see [sitting with tailbone pain](/blog/sitting-with-tailbone-pain.html)).
3. **Find out the direction.** An examination and a dynamic X-ray show whether the coccyx has moved inward or outward (see [tailbone subluxation](/blog/tailbone-subluxation-inward-or-outward.html)).
4. **Follow a plan made for you.** Once the coccyx is back in line, your exercises are chosen for your particular shift.

## After childbirth

New mothers are often told to start Kegels straight away. If you have tailbone pain after delivery, check with a specialist first: childbirth is one of the commonest causes of an inward-shifted coccyx (see [tailbone pain after pregnancy](/blog/tailbone-pain-after-pregnancy.html)).

## Sources

- [Dr Rajveer Singh's videos on tailbone pain (YouTube)](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCcLNy_lJceu4Ci8LaVW4GEw)
- [Neville CE et al. Association of coccygodynia with pelvic floor symptoms in women with pelvic pain. PM&R. 2022;14(11):1351–1359](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34533893/)

Source: https://tailbone.netlify.app/blog/tailbone-subluxation-inward-or-outward.html (published 2026-10-18)

# A displaced tailbone: why the direction of the shift matters

A displaced coccyx can be pushed inward into the pelvis or outward. Dr Rajveer Singh explains why the direction must be known first, how treatment differs, and how one patient recovered.

After a fall, a jolt or childbirth, the coccyx rarely breaks cleanly. More often it is pushed slightly out of line with the rest of the spine. This is called a **subluxation**, and it is one of the commonest reasons tailbone pain doesn't go away on its own.

## Key points

- A subluxed coccyx shifts in one of two directions: **inward** into the pelvis (anterior) or **outward** (posterior).
- The direction matters more than anything else, because the right treatment for one can make the other worse.
- Dr Rajveer checks the direction on a **dynamic X-ray** (taken sitting and standing) before any manipulation or exercise programme.
- Treatment then follows three steps: an exact diagnosis, internal manipulation to realign the coccyx, and exercises chosen for that direction.

## Inward or outward: what's the difference?

| What | Inward shift (anterior) | Outward shift (posterior) |
|---|---|---|
| Where the coccyx goes | Into the pelvis | Backwards, towards the skin |
| What makes it worse | Pressure from outside, and squeezing the pelvic floor | Direct pressure when sitting |
| Never do | Kegel or "butt-squeezing" exercises; external "bone setting" | Long sitting on flat, hard seats |
| Treatment | Internal manipulation, then exercises for an inward shift | Internal manipulation, then exercises for an outward shift |
Table: The two directions of tailbone subluxation, as Dr Rajveer Singh explains them.

## Why the X-ray comes first

From the outside, both kinds of subluxation can feel the same: pain on sitting, pain getting up, pain at the base of the spine. But they need opposite handling. A dynamic X-ray, taken sitting and standing, shows how the coccyx actually moves under your body weight. Dr Rajveer's rule is simple: no manipulation, no exercise programme and no physical therapy should begin without knowing the direction of the shift.

## The three steps of treatment

1. **Diagnose exactly.** The examination and a dynamic X-ray show whether the coccyx has shifted inward or outward, and by how much.
2. **Realign.** Internal manipulation gently moves the coccyx back into line. It is done in a short series of sessions, usually within about a week, spaced at the right intervals.
3. **Keep it there.** Exercises chosen for your direction of shift strengthen and relax the right muscles, so the coccyx stays in place. Doing them faithfully at home is what makes the result last.

## A patient's recovery

| When | What happened |
|---|---|
| Day 1 | An IT professional from Pune, badly affected by tailbone pain, was diagnosed with an outward (posterior) subluxation on a dynamic X-ray |
| Week 1 | A short series of internal manipulation sessions corrected the outward shift |
| Month 4 | Marked recovery, after following the home exercise programme very closely |
| Months 5 to 8 | He continued the exercises for another 3 to 4 months to keep the coccyx stable |
Table: One patient's recovery from an outward subluxation (shared by Dr Rajveer Singh).

Not everyone recovers at the same pace, but the pattern is typical: the manipulation corrects the position, and the exercises keep it.

## What to avoid while it heals

- Cycling and riding motorbikes, which put your weight on a narrow saddle right under the coccyx (see [two-wheelers and tailbone pain](/blog/two-wheeler-riding-and-tailbone-pain.html)).
- Sitting flat on hard chairs without a cut-out cushion (see [sitting with tailbone pain](/blog/sitting-with-tailbone-pain.html)).
- Bending forward without support.
- Squeezing exercises if your coccyx has shifted inward (see [Kegel exercises and tailbone pain](/blog/kegel-exercises-and-tailbone-pain.html)).
- External "bone setting" (see [why bone setting can be dangerous](/blog/tailbone-bone-setting-risks.html)).

## Treat it early

Tailbone pain is often brushed off as soreness that will pass. When the coccyx is out of line, it usually doesn't. Left alone, sitting at work, driving and even sleeping can become harder over months. Early assessment and the right treatment are much easier than undoing years of strain.

## Sources

- [Dr Rajveer Singh's videos on tailbone pain (YouTube)](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCcLNy_lJceu4Ci8LaVW4GEw)
- [Maigne JY et al. Causes and mechanisms of common coccydynia: role of body mass index and coccygeal trauma. Spine. 2000;25(23):3072–3079](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11145819/)
- [Garg B, Ahuja K. Coccydynia: a comprehensive review on etiology, radiological features and management options. J Clin Orthop Trauma. 2021;12(1):123–129](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7920198/)

# How coccydynia is treated, and how often each treatment works

Tailbone pain is treated in steps, from better sitting and hands-on care to injections and, rarely, surgery. What each step involves and the success rates reported in research.

Most people with tailbone pain get better without surgery. Treatment works like a ladder: start with the simplest, safest steps, and climb only if they don't help enough. Reviews put the success rate of the non-surgical steps at about **9 in 10**.

## Key points

- About **90%** of people with coccydynia improve with non-surgical care.
- The first step is changing **how and how long you sit**: a wedge or cut-out cushion, leaning forward, and regular breaks.
- Manipulation of the coccyx, usually combined with an injection, helped about **75–92%** of patients in older clinical series. General physiotherapy (heat, ultrasound) helped little in the same studies, so the type of hands-on treatment matters.
- Injections are an option when pain persists; reported relief varies widely between studies.
- Surgery (coccygectomy) is kept for a small, carefully selected group, and has a real risk of wound infection.

## The steps at a glance

| Step | What it involves | What studies report |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Sitting changes | Wedge or U-shaped (cut-out) cushion, leaning forward, breaks every 20–30 minutes | Recommended first-line in all reviews; a cut-out or wedge cushion is preferred over a doughnut ring (MSD Manual) |
| 2. Hands-on treatment | Internal or external manipulation of the coccyx, release of the pelvic floor muscles, stretching and exercises | Manipulation with injection cured about 85% in a 120-patient trial (Wray 1991); other series report 75–92% improvement (Perkins, Ramsey, summarised by Garg and Ahuja). The same trial found general physiotherapy of little help |
| 3. Medicines | Short courses of anti-inflammatory pain relief, sometimes medicines for nerve pain | Helpful for symptoms; not a cure on their own |
| 4. Injections | Local anaesthetic and steroid around the coccyx, or a ganglion impar block | About 60% responded to steroid and anaesthetic injections (Wray 1991); ganglion impar block helped 6 of 8 patients at 6 months in a small CT-guided study (Datir 2010) |
| 5. Ablation | Radiofrequency treatment of the nerves or the ganglion impar | Used for pain that keeps coming back after injections; evidence is from small studies |
| 6. Surgery | Removal of part or all of the coccyx (coccygectomy) | Needed by almost 20% in Wray's trial, with over 90% success; 85–100% improvement in carefully selected patients across studies; complication rates of 0–50% across studies, mostly wound infection |
Table: Coccydynia treatment options and reported results (Garg and Ahuja 2021, unless stated).

These figures come from different studies with different patients and definitions of success, so they can't be compared directly. They do show a clear pattern: the simple steps help most people, and the risky steps are only for a few.

## Step 1: sitting differently

Sitting puts weight on the coccyx, especially when you lean back. Small changes take that pressure off:

- Lean forward slightly so your weight rests on your thigh bones and sitting bones, not on the tailbone.
- Use a wedge or cut-out cushion with the gap at the back. A doughnut ring can still press on the coccyx.
- Stand up every 20–30 minutes, and avoid low, soft sofas.

See [sitting with tailbone pain](/blog/sitting-with-tailbone-pain.html) for more detail.

## Step 2: hands-on treatment

This is the core of what we do at the clinic. After a careful examination, the clinician gently moves the coccyx back towards its normal position and range of movement, and releases the tight pelvic floor muscles that pull on it (see [conditions linked to tailbone pain](/blog/conditions-linked-to-tailbone-pain.html)). Treatment is usually done from the inside, through the back passage, because that is the only way to reach the front of the coccyx and the muscles attached to it. It is explained fully before it starts, and you can stop at any time.

People whose coccyx is too mobile or slightly displaced when they sit often respond well. Those whose coccyx is very stiff may need more sessions or another step. This is one reason we [assess the coccyx shape and movement](/blog/coccyx-shapes-and-movement.html) first.

## Step 3: medicines

Anti-inflammatory tablets or gels can ease pain while other treatment takes effect. They are not a long-term answer, and should be taken only as advised by your doctor.

## Step 4: injections

If pain persists for several weeks despite the steps above, an injection of local anaesthetic and steroid around the painful joint can calm it down. Another option is a **ganglion impar block**, an injection at a small nerve cluster in front of the coccyx. Injections should be done by a specialist under X-ray or CT guidance.

## Steps 5 and 6: ablation and surgery

For the few people whose pain continues despite everything else, radiofrequency treatment of the nerves or removal of the coccyx may be considered. Surgery gives good results in carefully chosen patients, usually those with an unstable or clearly abnormal coccyx on sitting and standing X-rays. Because the wound is close to the back passage, infection is the main risk.

## Our approach

We start at the bottom of the ladder, with a thorough history and examination, sitting advice and hands-on treatment, and refer on only when it is genuinely needed. Most of our patients need only a few sessions. [Book a consultation](/book) in Delhi or online.

## Sources

- [Garg B, Ahuja K. Coccydynia: a comprehensive review on etiology, radiological features and management options. J Clin Orthop Trauma. 2021;12(1):123–129](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7920198/)
- [Lirette LS et al. Coccydynia: an overview of the anatomy, etiology, and treatment of coccyx pain. Ochsner J. 2014;14(1):84–87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3963058/)
- [Datir A, Connell D. CT-guided injection for ganglion impar blockade: a radiological approach to the management of coccydynia. Clin Radiol. 2010;65(1):21–25](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20103417/)
- [Wray CC et al. Coccydynia. Aetiology and treatment. J Bone Joint Surg Br. 1991;73(2):335–338](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2005168/)
- [MSD Manual Professional: Coccyx disorders (Foye PM, reviewed 2024)](https://www.msdmanuals.com/professional/musculoskeletal-and-connective-tissue-disorders/coccyx-disorders/coccyx-disorders)

# Tailbone pain in numbers

How common is tailbone pain, who gets it, what causes it and how often treatment works: the key figures from medical research, each with its source.

Coccydynia (tailbone or coccyx pain) is one of the most under-studied causes of back pain. This page brings together the numbers that are actually backed by published research, explains what they mean, and is honest about what is still unknown.

## Key points

- Nobody knows exactly how many people have coccydynia. It is thought to make up only around 1% of people seen for spine pain, but it is often missed or recorded as "low back pain".
- Women are affected about five times as often as men.
- Half or more of patients remember an injury such as a fall. Childbirth accounts for a smaller but important share in women.
- Body weight matters at both ends: both a high and a very low body mass index (BMI) raise the risk.
- About 9 in 10 people improve without surgery.

## The key figures at a glance

| Question | What research reports | Source |
|---|---|---|
| How common is it? | Exact incidence has not been reported; roughly 1% of people seen for musculoskeletal or spine pain | Lirette 2014; BMJ Best Practice |
| Women vs men | About 5 women for every man | Lirette 2014; Garg and Ahuja 2021 |
| Who gets it | Mostly adults and teenagers; uncommon in young children | Lirette 2014 |
| Remember an injury first | 50–65% of patients | Garg and Ahuja 2021 |
| Linked to childbirth | 7.3% of women's cases in one specialist clinic | Maigne 2012 |
| Abnormal coccyx movement when sitting | About 69% of patients on sitting and standing X-rays | Maigne 2000; Garg and Ahuja 2021 |
| Bony spur at the tip | About 14% of patients | Garg and Ahuja 2021 |
| Weight above which risk rises | BMI over 27.4 in women, over 29.4 in men | Garg and Ahuja 2021 |
| Better without surgery | About 90% | Lirette 2014; Garg and Ahuja 2021 |
Table: Coccydynia key figures. Full references are listed at the end of this article.

## Why the exact numbers are uncertain

Coccydynia rarely gets its own diagnosis code. In many records it is grouped with general low back pain, and many people never see a doctor about it, often out of embarrassment. That is why the reviews we rely on say plainly that its true incidence is unknown. Be wary of any website quoting a precise share of the population: we could not find a reliable source for such figures.

## Who is more likely to get it?

- Women, partly because of the shape of the pelvis and because of childbirth. See [why women get tailbone pain more often](/blog/why-women-get-tailbone-pain.html).
- People with a higher BMI, or who are very thin. See [body weight and tailbone pain](/blog/body-weight-and-tailbone-pain.html).
- People who sit for long hours or ride over rough roads. See [two-wheelers and tailbone pain](/blog/two-wheeler-riding-and-tailbone-pain.html).
- People with some other conditions, such as ankylosing spondylitis or pelvic floor problems. See [conditions linked to tailbone pain](/blog/conditions-linked-to-tailbone-pain.html).

## High rates in particular groups

Some studies have looked at specific groups of people. Their figures are much higher than the general rate, because these groups are exposed to particular risks. They should not be read as rates for a whole country.

| Group studied | Share with tailbone pain | Where and when | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| People with ankylosing spondylitis | 38.3% (vs 18.4% of women and 8% of men with ordinary back pain) | Istanbul, Turkey, 2014; 107 patients | Deniz 2014 |
| Women seeking physiotherapy for pelvic pain | 49.6% | USA, 2022; 127 women | Neville 2022 |
| Male motorbike riders | 33.2% | Pakistan, 2025; 190 riders | Fatima 2025 |
| Long-term wheelchair users | 76% | South Punjab, Pakistan, 2024; 250 users | Sanobar 2024 |
Table: Tailbone pain in specific study groups.

We have not found a published study measuring coccydynia across the general population of India. The two Pakistani studies are the closest regional data, and their settings (long sitting, motorbike commuting) are very familiar in Indian cities.

## How well does treatment work?

Most people get better with simple measures: a cut-out cushion, changes to how and how long they sit, and hands-on treatment of the coccyx and pelvic floor muscles. Injections are an option if pain persists, and surgery is kept for a small, carefully selected group. See [coccydynia treatment, step by step](/blog/coccydynia-treatment-ladder.html).

## Sources

- [Garg B, Ahuja K. Coccydynia: a comprehensive review on etiology, radiological features and management options. J Clin Orthop Trauma. 2021;12(1):123–129](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7920198/)

# 8 ways to sit more comfortably with tailbone pain

Desk job, long drives or a hard classroom bench? Small changes to how and how long you sit can take a lot of pressure off a sore coccyx.

If your tailbone hurts, sitting is usually the hardest part of the day. When you sit upright or lean back, part of your weight rests on the coccyx, the small bone at the very bottom of the spine. When it is bruised, inflamed or moving abnormally, that pressure turns into pain, and getting up from a chair can bring a sharp jolt.

How you sit makes a real difference. These are the changes our patients find most useful.

## 1. Lean slightly forward

Tilting your upper body a little forward shifts your weight onto your thigh bones and the "sitting bones" of your pelvis, and off the coccyx. Sitting on the front half of the chair with your feet flat on the floor makes this easier.

## 2. Use a cut-out cushion

A wedge or U-shaped cushion with a gap at the back lets the tailbone hang free instead of pressing on the seat. Round "doughnut" rings help some people but can still press on the coccyx, so a cushion with an open back is usually better. Take it with you: to the office, the car and restaurants.

What Dr Rajveer Singh looks for in a tailbone cushion:

| Feature | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| A cut-out or notch at the back | The tailbone doesn't touch the seat at all |
| Thicker at the back, thinner at the front | Lifts the pelvis and tips your weight forward onto the thighs |
| Firm foam, not soft memory foam | You don't sink down until the coccyx touches the chair again |
Table: Choosing a tailbone cushion. An ordinary soft pillow doesn't take the pressure off.

## 3. Choose firm seats over soft sofas

It sounds backwards, but deep, soft sofas let you sink and roll back onto the tailbone. A firm, supportive chair with a cushion is kinder.

## 4. Get up every 30 minutes

Pressure and stiffness build the longer you sit. Set a reminder to stand, walk a few steps or do a gentle stretch every half hour. On long drives, plan short breaks.

## 5. Stand up the smart way

Shift forward to the edge of the seat, bring your feet back under you, and push up through your legs while keeping your back straight. This avoids rocking back onto the coccyx at the moment you rise.

## 6. Support your lower back

A small cushion or rolled towel behind the lower back keeps you upright and stops you slumping, which tips weight back onto the tailbone.

## 7. Heat or ice

For a few minutes at a time, a warm pack can relax tight muscles around the coccyx, and an ice pack wrapped in a cloth can calm a flare-up. Use whichever helps you more.

## 8. Keep your bowels comfortable

Straining often makes tailbone pain worse. Plenty of water, fruit, vegetables and fibre help. If bowel movements are painful, ask your doctor or pharmacist about a gentle stool softener.

## When self-care isn't enough

Most tailbone pain settles with time and sensible habits. If yours hasn't improved after a few weeks, keeps coming back, or stops you working or sleeping, it is worth having the coccyx and surrounding muscles properly examined. A displaced or stiff coccyx, or tight pelvic-floor muscles, often needs hands-on treatment rather than more waiting.

See a doctor promptly if the pain comes with fever, numbness, leg weakness, or problems controlling your bladder or bowels.

## Sources

- [NHS: Tailbone (coccyx) pain](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/tailbone-coccyx-pain/)
- [Cleveland Clinic: Coccydynia (tailbone pain)](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/10436-coccydynia-tailbone-pain)

# Tailbone pain after having a baby

Many new mothers find that sitting to feed their baby is surprisingly painful. Here is why childbirth can affect the coccyx, and how it is treated.

Tailbone pain is much more common in women than in men, and pregnancy and childbirth are among the main reasons. Many mothers notice it in the weeks after delivery, often while sitting to feed the baby, which is exactly when sitting is hardest to avoid.

## Why pregnancy and childbirth affect the coccyx

- Hormones loosen the joints. During pregnancy, hormones relax the ligaments of the pelvis so the baby can pass through. The joint between the sacrum and the coccyx loosens too.
- The baby's head presses on the coccyx during a vaginal delivery, pushing it backwards. Occasionally the coccyx is bruised, strained or even displaced.
- Weight and posture change. Through pregnancy, the way you sit and stand changes, putting new strain on the lower spine and pelvic floor.
- Assisted or long deliveries and larger babies make injury a little more likely.

## What it typically feels like

- An ache or sharp pain right at the base of the spine
- Worse when sitting, especially leaning back, and when standing up
- Sometimes painful bowel movements or discomfort during intercourse

## What helps

1. **A cut-out (wedge or U-shaped) cushion** for feeding and for the car.
2. **Feeding positions that take weight off the tailbone:** lying on your side, or sitting leaning slightly forward with good back support.
3. **Gentle pelvic-floor exercises** once your midwife or doctor says it is safe.
4. **Keeping stools soft:** fluids and fibre, and avoiding straining.
5. **Heat or cold packs** for short periods.

Before taking pain relief while breastfeeding, check with your doctor or pharmacist which medicines are suitable.

## When to get it checked

Postnatal tailbone pain often eases over a few weeks, and in Dr Rajveer Singh's experience most of it settles within 3 to 4 months of delivery. If it is still there after about 4 months, keeps returning, or makes caring for your baby difficult, ask for an examination: the coccyx may have been pushed inward or outward during labour (see [tailbone subluxation](/blog/tailbone-subluxation-inward-or-outward.html)). When the coccyx has been pushed out of its normal position or the surrounding muscles stay in spasm, hands-on treatment can help a great deal, and you don't need to "just put up with it".

See a doctor urgently if you have fever, a wound or swelling near the tailbone, numbness, or new problems with bladder or bowel control.

## Sources

- [Cleveland Clinic: Coccydynia (tailbone pain)](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/10436-coccydynia-tailbone-pain)
- [NHS: Tailbone (coccyx) pain](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/tailbone-coccyx-pain/)

# When tailbone pain needs urgent attention

Most tailbone pain is mechanical and treatable without surgery. A few warning signs, though, mean you should see a doctor quickly. Here is what they are.

The vast majority of tailbone pain comes from a fall, childbirth, long sitting or strain on the coccyx and the muscles around it. It is uncomfortable and can be stubborn, but it isn't dangerous. Rarely, though, pain at the base of the spine is a sign of something that needs prompt medical care.

## See a doctor promptly if you have tailbone pain with:

- Fever, chills or feeling generally unwell. This could mean an infection, such as an abscess or an infected cyst near the tailbone (a pilonidal cyst).
- A lump, swelling, redness or a wound near the tailbone.
- Unexplained weight loss, or a history of cancer. Very occasionally, a growth in or near the sacrum or coccyx causes pain.
- Pain that is severe and getting steadily worse, or pain that is just as bad lying down at night.
- Pain after a major accident such as a road traffic collision or a fall from height, where a fracture is possible.

## Go to an emergency department straight away if you have:

- Numbness around the buttocks, genitals or inner thighs (sometimes called "saddle" numbness)
- New difficulty passing urine, or loss of bladder or bowel control
- Weakness in one or both legs

These can be signs of pressure on the nerves at the bottom of the spinal canal, which needs urgent assessment.

## Why a proper examination matters

Because so many conditions can cause pain low in the back and pelvis, a specialist first takes a careful history and examines the coccyx, the joints around it and the pelvic muscles. When needed, X-rays taken sitting and standing can show whether the coccyx moves abnormally, and an MRI can rule out other causes. Only once the cause is clear should treatment begin.

If none of the warning signs above apply, tailbone pain is usually treatable with self-care and targeted, hands-on therapy. Surgery is rarely needed.

## Sources

- [Cleveland Clinic: Coccydynia (tailbone pain)](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/10436-coccydynia-tailbone-pain)
- [NHS: Tailbone (coccyx) pain](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/tailbone-coccyx-pain/)

# What happens at a coccydynia consultation (and how to prepare)

Nervous about your first visit for tailbone pain? Here is what to expect, step by step, and how to prepare so you get the most from the appointment.

Many people put off getting tailbone pain checked because they aren't sure what the visit involves, or they feel embarrassed. Knowing what happens makes it much easier.

## Before you come

- Make a list of your medicines and any past operations or injuries.
- Note how your pain behaves: when it started, what makes it worse (sitting, getting up, driving, bowel movements) and what helps.
- Wear comfortable clothes.
- If you would prefer to be seen by a **female clinician**, mention it when booking.

## 1. Listening and history

The visit starts with a conversation: how the pain began (a fall, childbirth, long sitting or no clear reason), how long you have had it, how it affects your work, sleep and daily life, and what you have already tried.

## 2. Examination

The clinician examines your lower back, pelvis and the area around the tailbone, checking for tenderness, swelling and how the coccyx and surrounding muscles respond to pressure and movement. Everything is explained first, and nothing happens without your consent. You can ask to pause at any time.

## 3. Pinpointing the cause

The aim is to find out what is actually causing the pain: whether the coccyx is moving too much, too little or sitting out of position, whether the pelvic-floor muscles are in spasm, or whether something else needs ruling out.

## 4. Treatment plan

You'll leave with a clear plan. Depending on the cause, this may include hands-on treatment such as manipulation of the coccyx and its muscles, together with posture and seating advice, a suitable cushion, and exercises you can do at home. Many patients notice a difference early, but the plan is always tailored to your own situation.

## 5. Follow-up

After treatment, a short check-in a week or two later helps track your pain and sitting tolerance, so the plan can be adjusted if needed.
